memoryText: You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive.
readingInstruction: Today there is no new reading. Yesterday closed Unit 3 with the review of the entire patriarchal narrative. Today closes the week with rest. The book of Genesis is now behind you. Take time today to feel the weight of what you have read, and to anticipate the Exodus to come.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Genesis 50:20 is the theological climax of the entire patriarchal narrative, and of the entire book of Genesis. It is two sentences in one.

“You meant evil against me”, the brothers’ sin was real. Joseph does not minimize what they did. There is no false forgiveness here, no pretending nothing happened.

“But God meant it for good”, behind their wickedness, God was working. Moving the pieces. Positioning Joseph in Egypt so that, when the famine came, many lives could be preserved. The same event was both wicked (on the brothers’ part) and providential (on God’s). Both are true at once.

This will eventually be said about the cross. The crucifixion of Christ was the most evil act in human history. It was also the most loving act of God in history. The same event. Both sentences true.

Carry this verse through your week. When you face injustice, remember it. When you mourn a wrong done to you, remember it. The God who turned Joseph’s pit into a throne can do the same with your story.
weekInReview:
This week closed the patriarchal era and the book of Genesis. You read Judah’s plea for Benjamin, the brother who once proposed selling Joseph now offering himself for the youngest. You watched Joseph reveal himself, weep, and forgive. You traveled with the family of Jacob down to Egypt and settled in Goshen. You read Jacob’s prophetic blessings on his twelve sons, including the famous promise that the scepter would not depart from Judah. You watched Joseph die, his bones placed in a coffin in Egypt, awaiting the Exodus four hundred years later. You worshiped with Psalm 47 (God’s reign over the nations) and the opening of Psalm 66 (all the earth called to praise). And yesterday you completed the Unit 3 review, anchored on Genesis 15:6, justification by faith.

Genesis is over. The patriarchal family is in Egypt. The four-hundred-year sojourning has begun. And the Lion of Judah stands over everything still to come.
reflectionQuestions: Looking back at Genesis as a whole, where did your understanding of God deepen most? You have walked through 50 chapters in about 9 weeks. The book introduced God as Creator, Judge, Covenant-maker, Provider, the God of the patriarchs. Which face of God did you most need to see in this season of your life? Why?

How does Genesis 50:20 prepare you to read about the cross? When you reach the Gospels later in this plan, you will encounter the most evil act ever committed, and the most loving act God ever performed, in the same event. Joseph’s words to his brothers are the theological key. Sit with this. How does the resurrection prove that what humans meant for evil, God meant for good?

What patriarchal failure most resembles your own? Genesis is candid about the failures of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph’s brothers. Lies. Favoritism. Manipulation. Betrayal. Drift. Where do you see your own story in theirs? And where do you see God’s grace operating despite their (and your) failures?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for what you have seen of his hand through the book of Genesis.
Thank him that what others meant for evil he meant for good, supremely at the cross.
Ask him to give you Joseph’s eyes for what lies ahead.
